function statusOf(report: CheckReport, id: string): RefStatus['status'] {
  const c = report.nodes[id] ?? report.edges[id] ?? report.absences[id];
  return c ? c.status : 'unknown';
}

export async function answer(o: AnswerOptions): Promise<{ answer: Answer; map: CodeMap; report: CheckReport; sessionId: string | null }> {
  const before = check(o.map, o.root);
  const selection = selectionLines(o.map, o.selection);
  const status = (text: string) => o.onProgress?.({ kind: 'status', text });
  const live0 = mapIds(o.map);
  let cost = 0;
  let missing = '';

  if (o.quick !== false) {
    status('Answering from the map');
    try {
      const res = await o.agent({
        prompt: quickAnswerPrompt(o.map, before, selection, o.question, citedExcerpts(o.root, o.map, o.selection), o.earlier ?? []),
        schema: QUICK_ANSWER_SCHEMA,
        cwd: o.root,
        tools: [],
        resume: null,
        model: o.model,
        maxTurns: 3,
        signal: o.signal,
      });
      cost += res.cost ?? 0;
      const quick = RawQuickAnswer.safeParse(res.output);
      if (quick.success && quick.data.answered && quick.data.concept.trim()) {
        const q = quick.data;
        const result: Answer = {
          id: `ans-${crypto.randomBytes(4).toString('hex')}`,
          question: o.question,
          selection: o.selection,
          concept: q.concept,
          how: q.how,
          code: q.code,
          refs: [...new Set(q.refs)].map((id) => ({ id, status: statusOf(before, id) })),
          followUps: q.followUps,
          moves: {
            focus: q.moves?.focus && live0.has(q.moves.focus) ? q.moves.focus : null,
            highlight: (q.moves?.highlight ?? []).filter((id) => live0.has(id)),
          },
          added: [],
          problems: [],
          fix: null,
          source: 'map',
          cost,
        };
        // The map didn't change, and the explainer session (what Claude has read in the code) carries on as it was.
        return { answer: result, map: o.map, report: before, sessionId: o.session };
      }
      if (quick.success) missing = quick.data.missing;
    } catch (err) {
      if (o.signal?.aborted) throw err;
      // A failed quick try isn't the end: Claude with the code still gets the question.
      cost += (err as { cost?: number }).cost ?? 0;
    }
    status('The map doesn\'t cover this, so Claude is looking in the code');
  }

  const res = await o.agent({
    prompt: explainerPrompt(o.map, before, selection, o.question, missing),
    schema: ANSWER_SCHEMA,
    cwd: o.root,
    resume: o.session,
    model: o.model,
    onProgress: o.onProgress,
    signal: o.signal,
  });
  const parsed = RawAnswer.safeParse(res.output);
  if (!parsed.success) throw new Error(`Claude's answer couldn't be read: ${parsed.error.issues.slice(0, 3).map((i) => i.message).join('; ')}`);
  const raw = parsed.data;

  const problems: string[] = [];
  let map = o.map;
  let added: string[] = [];
  if (raw.add) {
    const merged = addToMap(o.map, raw.add);
    if (merged.ok) {
      const old = mapIds(o.map);
      added = [...mapIds(merged.map)].filter((id) => !old.has(id));
      map = merged.map;
    } else {
      problems.push(...merged.problems.map((p) => `Not added to the map: ${p}`));
    }
  }

  let report = check(map, o.root);
  const failed = added.filter((id) => statusOf(report, id) === 'unconfirmed');
  if (failed.length) {
    for (const id of failed) {
      const c = report.nodes[id] ?? report.edges[id] ?? report.absences[id];
      problems.push(`Not drawn, couldn't confirm ${id}: ${c?.reasons.join('; ') ?? 'unknown'}`);
    }
    map = removeFromMap(map, new Set(failed));
    report = check(map, o.root);
    const live = mapIds(map);
    added = added.filter((id) => live.has(id));
  }

  let fix: FixProposal | null = null;
  if (raw.fix) {
    const proposed = proposeFix(o.root, map, raw.fix);
    if (proposed.ok) fix = proposed.proposal;
    else problems.push(...proposed.problems.map((p) => `The proposed fix can't be applied: ${p}`));
  }

  const live = mapIds(map);
  const result: Answer = {
    id: `ans-${crypto.randomBytes(4).toString('hex')}`,
    question: o.question,
    selection: o.selection,
    concept: raw.concept,
    how: raw.how,
    code: raw.code,
const ANSWER_DEPTHS = [
  '- `concept`: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. `how`: the mechanism; define any term you use. `code`: function names, files and lines.',
  '- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.',
];

/** The first, cheap try: answer from the map and the code around its citations, with no tools. */
export function quickAnswerPrompt(
  map: CodeMap,
  report: CheckReport,
  selection: readonly SelectionLine[],
  question: string,
  excerpts: string,
  earlier: readonly { question: string; concept: string }[],
): string {
  return [
    'You answer questions about a code map for someone semi-technical, using only the map and the code excerpts below. You have no tools: you can\'t read more of the repo.',
    '',
    ...questionContext(map, report, selection, question),
    '',
    earlier.length ? `## Asked earlier on this map\n${earlier.map((e) => `- "${e.question}": ${e.concept}`).join('\n')}\n` : '',
    '## Code around what the map cites',
    excerpts || '(none)',
    '',
    '## First decide whether you can answer from this alone',
    '- `answered: true` only if the map and the excerpts fully answer the question, without guessing about code you can\'t see.',
    '- `answered: false` if answering needs code that isn\'t shown, if they ask for a change or fix, or if a good answer would add boxes or arrows to the map. Then say in `missing`, in one sentence, what you would need to look at, and leave the other fields empty. Someone with the whole repo picks it up from there.',
    '',
    '## How to answer (when `answered` is true)',
    ...ANSWER_DEPTHS,
    '- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.',
    '- `followUps`: up to 3 short next questions.',
  ].join('\n');
}

export function explainerPrompt(map: CodeMap, report: CheckReport, selection: readonly SelectionLine[], question: string, missing = ''): string {
  return [
    'You answer questions about a code map for someone semi-technical. You can Read, Grep and Glob the repo; you cannot edit anything.',
    '',
    ...questionContext(map, report, selection, question),
    ...(missing ? ['', `## Why the map alone wasn't enough\n${missing}`] : []),
    '',
    '## How to answer',
    ...ANSWER_DEPTHS,
    '- If the map doesn\'t cover it, explore, then put what you found in `add` (new areas, nodes, edges or absences with evidence, same rules as the map; ids must be new). Connect new boxes to existing ones with arrows where the code really connects them.',
    '- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.',
    '- If they ask for a change, don\'t edit (you can\'t). Propose a `fix`: codemap shows it to them on the map, and if they approve, codemap applies exactly your edits and re-checks the map. So describe it as a proposal waiting for their approval, never as something for them to apply by hand.',
    '- The `fix`: `summary` in plain words; `edits` as exact replacements (`find` copied exactly from the file, occurring once; `replace` is the new text); `creates` for new files. If the fix creates a connection between two boxes, fill `connects` with `from`, `to`, a short `label`, and `evidenceFile` + `evidenceText` (text that will appear in the new code). Keep fixes small and in the style of the surrounding code.',
    '- `followUps`: up to 3 short next questions.',
    '',
    ...EVIDENCE_RULES,
  ].join('\n');
}

// A question about a different part of the app, over HTTP: the offer, a new map linked back to this one, or an answer
// in words that draws nothing here.
import { join } from 'node:path';
import WebSocket from 'ws';
import { afterAll, beforeAll, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { ANSWER_SCHEMA } from '../src/schemas';
import { startServer, type CodemapServer, type ServerEvent } from '../src/server';
import { CARE_MAP, cleanup, copyCareApp, scriptedAgent, waitFor } from './helpers';

const elsewhere = () => ({ route: 'elsewhere', newQuestion: 'How do invoices get sent?' });
const agent = scriptedAgent([
  () => CARE_MAP, // the first map
  elsewhere, // "and invoices?" on it
  () => CARE_MAP, // the new map they said yes to
  elsewhere, // asked again
  () => ({ concept: 'Nothing in this app sends invoices.' }), // …and this time answered in words
]);

let server: CodemapServer;
let ws: WebSocket;
const events: ServerEvent[] = [];
const api = async (method: string, path: string, body?: unknown) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${server.url}${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: { 'x-codemap-token': server.token, 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  return { status: res.status, body: (await res.json()) as any };
};
const answers = () => events.filter((e): e is Extract<ServerEvent, { type: 'answer' }> => e.type === 'answer');
const made = (id: string) => waitFor(() => events.find((e) => e.type === 'job' && e.job === 'make' && e.mapId === id && e.status === 'done'));

beforeAll(async () => {
  const root = copyCareApp();
  server = await startServer({ root, port: 0, agent, viewerDir: join(root, 'no-viewer') });
  ws = new WebSocket(`ws://127.0.0.1:${server.port}/ws?t=${server.token}`);
  ws.on('message', (d) => events.push(JSON.parse(String(d))));
  await new Promise((r) => ws.once('open', r));
});
afterAll(async () => {
  ws.close();
  await server.close();
  cleanup();
});

describe('a question about a different part of the app', () => {
  let mapId = '';

  it('offers a new map instead of answering, and makes one linked back when they say yes', async () => {
    mapId = (await api('POST', '/api/maps', { question: 'What happens when a patient converts?' })).body.id;
    await made(mapId);
    await api('POST', `/api/maps/${mapId}/ask`, { question: 'and invoices?', selection: {} });
    const offered = (await waitFor(() => answers()[0])).answer;
    expect(offered.offer).toEqual({ question: 'How do invoices get sent?', existing: null, status: 'pending', mapId: null });

    expect((await api('POST', `/api/maps/${mapId}/answers/${offered.id}/offer`, { choice: 'maybe' })).status).toBe(400);
    const yes = await api('POST', `/api/maps/${mapId}/answers/${offered.id}/offer`, { choice: 'map' });
    expect(yes.status).toBe(200);
    const newId = yes.body.id as string;
    await made(newId);
    const child = await api('GET', `/api/maps/${newId}`);
    expect(child.body.meta.question).toBe('How do invoices get sent?');
    expect(child.body.meta.parent).toEqual({ mapId, question: CARE_MAP.question });

    const parent = await api('GET', `/api/maps/${mapId}`);
    expect(parent.body.answers[0].offer).toMatchObject({ status: 'mapped', mapId: newId }); // saved, so a reload shows it
    expect(events).toContainEqual(expect.objectContaining({ type: 'answerUpdate', mapId, answer: expect.objectContaining({ id: offered.id }) }));
    expect((await api('POST', `/api/maps/${mapId}/answers/${offered.id}/offer`, { choice: 'map' })).status).toBe(404); // only once
  });

  it('answers in words from the code when they say no, drawing nothing on this map', async () => {

    await api('POST', `/api/maps/${mapId}/ask`, { question: 'and invoices?', selection: {} });

    expect(after.body.answers.map((a: any) => a.offer?.status ?? null)).toEqual(['mapped', 'answered', null]);
  });
});

// Moving between the home page and maps without reloading the page, so the connection to codemap (and what's on screen)
// carries over. Links inside the app are plain <a href>s; a click on one is turned into a navigation here.
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function navigate(url: string) {
  if (url === `${location.pathname}${location.search}`) return;
  history.pushState(null, '', url);
  window.dispatchEvent(new PopStateEvent('popstate'));
}

/** The current path, kept up to date through back/forward and `navigate`, with in-app link clicks taken over. */
export function usePath(): string {
  const [path, setPath] = useState(location.pathname);
  useEffect(() => {
    const onPop = () => setPath(location.pathname);
    const onClick = (e: MouseEvent) => {
      if (e.defaultPrevented || e.button !== 0 || e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey || e.shiftKey || e.altKey) return;
      const a = (e.target as Element | null)?.closest?.('a[href]');
      if (!(a instanceof HTMLAnchorElement) || a.target || a.origin !== location.origin) return;
      e.preventDefault();
      navigate(`${a.pathname}${a.search}`);
    };
    window.addEventListener('popstate', onPop);
    document.addEventListener('click', onClick);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('popstate', onPop);
      document.removeEventListener('click', onClick);
    };
  }, []);
  return path;
}

It's built: Claude now decides, in the call that already runs first, whether a question gets an answer from the map, a search of the code, or the offer of a new map. All 131 tests pass, 9 of them new, and typecheck is clean. I checked the routing with real Claude and the new screens in Chrome.

**How it works:**
- **Three routes in the first call.** Claude sees the map, the code around its citations, and the list of other saved maps, and returns one of:
  - **Answer:** the map covers it, so you get an answer in words plus highlights.
  - **Search the code:** it's about this map's flow but needs code the map doesn't show. The search runs and can add checked boxes.
  - **Different part of the app:** a card asks "Make a new map for this?". If a saved map already covers the question, it offers "Open that map" instead.
- **Your choice on the card:**
  - **Make a new map for this:** the map starts and the tab switches to it without reloading. The new map remembers where it came from, and the top bar links back ("← What happens w…").
  - **Just answer in words:** Claude reads the code and answers, but nothing is drawn or proposed on the current map.
- **One rule in plain code:** if you've selected something on the map, the question is about this map, so it never offers a new one.
- **Top bar:** a map switcher (a dropdown of every map in the repo, including ones being made) and a "＋ New map" button. Browser back and forward work too.

**Real routing check** (first call only, on the care-app test project, with a fake saved "invoices" map):

Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnzhang/.claude/skills/codemap

# codemap

codemap turns a question about this repo into a map the person can explore in their browser: areas of the app, the
steps in order, labeled arrows, and red dashed arrows where something that should be connected isn't. A plain program
checks every claim against the code before it's shown. In the map they can take a walkthrough, select any box or arrow
and ask about it, and approve fixes that codemap applies and re-checks.

## When to use it

- The user asks how something works across several files: "what happens when…", "how does X reach Y", "where does Z
  get triggered".
- The user is about to change code they don't understand yet and wants to see it first.
- The user asks for a map, diagram, graph or walkthrough of part of the code.

Don't use it for a question about a single line or function; answer that directly.

## How to run it

Run from the repo root (or pass `--repo`). Use the user's question in their own words:

```bash
codemap "What happens when a patient converts?" --repo "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
```

It starts a small local server and opens the map in the user's browser by itself, where they watch Claude explore
(about a minute for a small repo). Don't pass `--no-open`. It also prints the link
(`http://127.0.0.1:4317/m/<id>?t=<token>`): tell the user the map is opening, and give them the link in case the tab
didn't appear. Run the command in the background and don't wait for it to exit. Don't stop it yourself either: it stops
on its own a little after the user closes the last codemap tab (never while Claude is still working), or when they
press Stop codemap on the page. If a codemap server is already running, the new one picks another free port.

Other commands:

- `codemap open` lists the maps already made in this repo (they're saved under `.codemap/maps/`).
- `codemap check <map-id>` re-checks a saved map against the current code and prints anything that no longer holds.
  It exits with 1 if a claim fails, so it can run in CI.

## Notes

- codemap reads the code and never changes it, except for a fix the user approves in the map.
- It never reads secret files (`.env`, keys) and only listens on 127.0.0.1.
- It needs Claude access: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or a logged-in Claude Code.
- If `codemap` isn't on the PATH, it hasn't been installed. Tell the user to install it from the codemap repo
  (see its README) instead of guessing another command.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-04 03:54:20Z)**_

Here's what each one does, left to right:

| Item | What it does | Also available elsewhere? |
|---|---|---|
| **codemap** (logo) | Goes to the home page: your maps, and a box to start a new one | Same place as "＋ New map" |
| **◀ ▶** | Back and forward through where the map was looking (highlights and focus after answers or walkthrough stops). Not browser back. | Easy to confuse with browser back |
| **Question ▾** | Switches to another map in this repo | |
| **＋ New map** | Goes to the home page to ask a new question | Same as the logo |
| **✓ 18 of 26 confirmed** | Not a button: how many of the map's claims the checker confirmed | |
| **Jump to…** | Type a step's name to find and focus it | Rarely needed on a 5–12-box map |
| **Whole map** | Closes the answer and clears highlighting | Esc, and the × on the answer |
| **Pick** | Drag-select mode: draw a box around several steps to ask about them | Shift-click picks several too |
| **Walkthrough / Leave walkthrough** | Starts or leaves the walkthrough | "Take the walkthrough" in the side panel; Done or Esc to leave |
| **Stop codemap** | Shuts down the local server | Codemap stops on its own about 30 seconds after you close the tab |
| **Green dot** | Connected to codemap | |

You're right that it's a lot: about half of these duplicate something else or are rarely used. What I'd do:
- **Remove:** ◀ ▶ (Esc and "Whole map" cover going back), the Walkthrough button (the side panel has it), and "Stop codemap" (tab close handles it; I'd keep it on the home page only).
- **Merge:** keep "＋ New map". The logo can stay as the home link, but drop the separate button or the logo, whichever you prefer.
- **Shrink:** "Jump to…" becomes a small search icon, or the `/` key. "Pick" becomes Shift-drag on the canvas, with no button. "Whole map" moves into the zoom controls in the canvas corner, next to fit-to-screen.
- **Green dot:** show it only when the connection drops.

The top bar would then be: **codemap · Question ▾ · ＋ New map · ✓ confirmed · ⌕**.

Shift-drag needs checking that React Flow supports it without clashing with panning. I'd check its docs rather than guess.

Separately: that map shows 8 claims it couldn't confirm. That's most likely because the code changed after it was drawn: today's edits to the answer code, plus the other session's. Codemap is doing its job there; re-asking the question would draw a fresh map.

Want me to make the trim as described, or keep any of those buttons?

function FixCard({ fix, onApprove, onReject, onUndo, map }: { fix: FixState; map: CodeMap; onApprove: () => void; onReject: () => void; onUndo: () => void }) {
  const p = fix.proposal;
  const dirty = p.files.filter((f) => f.uncommitted);
  if (fix.status === 'applied') {
    return (
      <Card eyebrow="Fix applied · re-checked" tone="ok">
        <ul className="progress">
          <li><span className="ic">✓</span>Changed {p.files.length} {p.files.length === 1 ? 'file' : 'files'}: {p.files.map((f) => f.file).join(', ')}</li>
          <li><span className="ic">✓</span>Re-checked the map against the new code</li>
          {fix.edgeId && <li><span className="ic">✓</span>New confirmed connection: {nameOf(map, fix.edgeId)}</li>}
          {fix.closed.length > 0 && <li><span className="ic">✓</span>Closed: {fix.closed.length === 1 ? 'the missing connection' : `${fix.closed.length} missing connections`}</li>}
        </ul>
        {fix.undoable
          ? <div className="btns"><button className="btn" onClick={onUndo}>Undo this fix</button></div>
          : <p className="muted small">Undo was available until codemap stopped. To reverse it now, use git.</p>}
      </Card>
    );
  }
  if (fix.status === 'rejected' || fix.status === 'undone') {
    return <Card eyebrow={fix.status === 'undone' ? 'Fix undone' : 'Fix rejected'}><p className="muted">{p.summary}</p>{fix.status === 'undone' && <div className="btns"><button className="btn" onClick={onApprove}>Apply it again</button></div>}</Card>;
  }
  return (
    <Card eyebrow={`Proposed fix · ${p.files.length} ${p.files.length === 1 ? 'file' : 'files'} · nothing changed yet`} tone="ai">
      <p>{p.summary}</p>
      {p.connects && <p className="muted small">The green dashed arrow on the map is the connection this would create.</p>}
      <pre className="diff">{p.diff.split('\n').map((l, i) => <span key={i} className={l.startsWith('+ ') ? 'add' : l.startsWith('- ') ? 'del' : l.includes(' · ') ? 'file' : ''}>{l}{'\n'}</span>)}</pre>
      {dirty.length > 0 ? (
        <p className="warn small">⚠ {dirty.map((f) => f.file).join(', ')} {dirty.length === 1 ? 'has' : 'have'} uncommitted changes. They'll be kept; the fix applies on top.</p>
      ) : (
        <div className="chips"><span className="chip static"><span className="tick">✓</span>no uncommitted changes in these files</span></div>
      )}
      {fix.problems.length > 0 && <ul className="problems">{fix.problems.map((x) => <li key={x}>{x}</li>)}</ul>}
      <div className="btns">
        <button className="btn primary" disabled={fix.status === 'applying'} onClick={onApprove}>{fix.status === 'applying' ? 'Applying…' : 'Approve'}</button>
        <button className="btn" onClick={onReject}>Reject</button>
      </div>
      <p className="muted small">Codemap writes exactly this change, then re-checks the map. It won't apply if these files change first.</p>
    </Card>
  );
}

            {s.answers.slice().reverse().map((a) => (
              <li key={a.id}><button className={cls('link-btn', a.id === s.shown && 'on')} onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'show', answerId: a.id })}>{a.question}</button></li>
            ))}

/** "This looks like a different part of the app": a new map for it (or the one that already covers it), or words. */
function OfferCard({ answer, map, busy, onOffer, onClose }: { answer: Answer; map: CodeMap; busy: boolean; onOffer: (answerId: string, choice: 'map' | 'words') => void; onClose: () => void }) {
  const o = answer.offer!;
  if (o.status === 'mapped') {
    return (
      <Card eyebrow="A different part of the app" title={`“${answer.question}”`} onClose={onClose}>
        <p className="muted">You made a new map for this.</p>
        {o.mapId && <div className="btns"><a className="btn primary" href={pageUrl(o.mapId)}>Open it</a></div>}
      </Card>
    );
  }
  if (o.status === 'answered') {
    return (
      <Card eyebrow="A different part of the app" title={`“${answer.question}”`} onClose={onClose}>
        <p className="muted">You chose an answer in words, without adding to this map. It's in the list of questions below.</p>
      </Card>
    );
  }
  return (
    <Card eyebrow="A different part of the app" title={`“${answer.question}”`} tone="ai" onClose={onClose}>
      <p>This map is about “{map.question}”. Your question looks like it's about something else, so it wouldn't fit here.</p>
      {o.existing && <p>There's already a map for it: “{o.existing.question}”.</p>}
      <div className="btns">
        {o.existing && <a className="btn primary" href={pageUrl(o.existing.id)}>Open that map</a>}
        <button className={o.existing ? 'btn' : 'btn primary'} onClick={() => onOffer(answer.id, 'map')}>Make a new map for this</button>
        <button className="btn" disabled={busy} onClick={() => onOffer(answer.id, 'words')} title={busy ? 'Claude is still working on this map' : undefined}>Just answer in words</button>
      </div>
      <p className="muted small">A new map takes a minute or two. An answer in words reads the code but adds nothing to this map.</p>
    </Card>
  );
}

/** What answers added, as layers to show or hide. Hiding them all shows the map as it was first drawn. */
function Layers({ state, dispatch }: { state: State; dispatch: Dispatch<Action> }) {
  const layers = layersOf(state);
  if (!layers.length) return null;
  const allHidden = layers.every((l) => !l.visible);
  return (
    <Card eyebrow="Added by your questions">
      <ul className="layers">
        {layers.map((l) => (
          <li key={l.answerId}>
            <label>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={l.visible} onChange={(e) => dispatch({ type: 'layer', answerId: l.answerId, visible: e.target.checked })} />
              <span className="layer-n">+{l.ids.length}</span>
              <span className="layer-q">{l.question}</span>
            </label>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <div className="btns">
        <button className="btn" onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'allLayers', visible: allHidden })}>{allHidden ? 'Show everything' : 'Show the original map'}</button>
      </div>
    </Card>
  );
}

function Selected({ map, report, ids, depth, dispatch }: { map: CodeMap; report: CheckReport | null; ids: string[]; depth: Depth; dispatch: Dispatch<Action> }) {
  if (ids.length > 1) {
    return (
      <Card eyebrow={`${ids.length} selected`}>
        <Chips map={map} report={report} ids={ids.map((id) => ({ id, status: checkOf(report, id)?.status ?? 'unknown' }))} onPick={() => undefined} />
        <p className="muted small">Ask about them together in the box below.</p>
      </Card>
    );
  }
  const id = ids[0]!;
  const node = map.nodes.find((n) => n.id === id);
  const edge = map.edges.find((e) => e.id === id);
  const gap = map.absences.find((a) => a.id === id);
  const c = checkOf(report, id);
  const evidence = node?.evidence ?? edge?.evidence ?? [];
  const evidenceChecks = c && 'evidence' in c && c.evidence ? c.evidence : [];
  return (
    <Card eyebrow={node ? 'Step' : edge ? 'Connection' : 'Missing connection'} title={nameOf(map, id)} tone={gap ? 'dead' : undefined}>
      {node?.explain && <Depths depth={depth} dispatch={dispatch} texts={node.explain} />}
      {gap && <p>The code has no connection here. Codemap re-ran the search <code>{gap.search.pattern}</code>{gap.search.paths ? <> in <code>{gap.search.paths.join(', ')}</code></> : null} and found {report?.absences[gap.id]?.found ?? '?'} {report?.absences[gap.id]?.found === 1 ? 'match' : 'matches'}.</p>}
      {c && c.status !== 'confirmed' && <div className="warn small">Couldn't confirm against the code: {c.reasons.join('; ')}</div>}
      {evidence.length > 0 && (
        <div className="basis">
          <div className="eyebrow">Where it is in the code</div>
          <div className="chips">
            {evidence.map((e, i) => {
              const ok = evidenceChecks[i]?.ok ?? false;
              return <span key={i} className={cls('chip static', !ok && 'chip-unconfirmed')}><span className={ok ? 'tick' : 'qmark'}>{ok ? '✓' : '?'}</span>{e.file}:{evidenceChecks[i]?.foundAt ?? e.line}</span>;
            })}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
      <p className="muted small">Ask about it in the box below.</p>
    </Card>
  );
}

## What I notice
1. **The pain grows with distance from the code, not with skill.** The integration consultant (working in a client's codebase), Jay (whose technical cofounder owns the backend) and Pat (whose system got so big he needed a "design bible") all hit it. What they have in common is code they didn't write, or a system too big to hold in their head. Patrick, building his own small thing, mostly doesn't feel it.
2. **Patrick is a warning, not a customer, for now.** He doesn't care how things are wired; he cares about users and shipping, and occasional breakage is fine at his scale. That's the strongest counter-signal so far: early builders may have no reason to understand their backend. It supports the `HANDOFF.md` guess that the pain arrives with users, teammates or clients' codebases.
3. **Diagrams as a steering wheel, not a document.** Patrick already has Claude draw dependency graphs and UML, then edits by pointing ("remove the GitHub connection"). That's codemap's fix-from-the-map idea, done by hand with unchecked diagrams.
4. **The frontend-leaning people think in user journeys.** Pat wants user flows and personas; Jay struggles with UX flow. Neither naturally thinks in backend boxes.
5. **Watching an agent build is its own pain.** Pat lets an agent run for an hour and gets something completely wrong. That's the "live agent activity on the map" idea from `HANDOFF.md`, and it's a different product moment: during the build, not after.
6. **Walls of text are the shared enemy.** The consultant said it most directly, and it's the clearest match for what codemap does today.

## How different would mapping user journeys be?
Less different than it sounds for the map itself, much more different for live renderings.

**A journey map from the code (no running app)** is close to what codemap does now:

| | Backend map (today) | Journey map |
|---|---|---|
| Areas | Parts of the system | Screens or pages |
| Boxes | Steps in the code | Things the user does (click Convert, fill the form) |
| Arrows | Calls, requests, events | Navigation (this button goes to that page), plus the request each action sends |
| What plain code can check | Calls, imports, request → route | Routes and pages exist, links and redirects point at real routes, click handlers send real requests |
| Gaps | "Nothing listens for this event" | "This button goes nowhere", "this page has no way back", "this form's request matches no route" |

The code-facts package already finds entry points like `PatientHeader` and links requests from the frontend to backend routes. That link is the bridge: a journey map on top, and selecting an action could open the backend map for what it triggers. That's also a nice answer for Jay: one map for him (the journey), connected to one for his cofounder (the backend).

**Live renderings, pointing at the real UI** are a different kind of system:
- **It has to run the app.** Today codemap only reads code. Running an app means a dev server, a database with sample data, login, environment variables (codemap never reads secrets), and executing the user's code. That's a real change in what codemap promises, and every framework does it differently.
- **It needs screen-to-code mapping.** "This button is `PatientHeader.tsx` line 12" works in development builds through a compiler plugin that tags elements with their source file. It's doable but framework-specific: one approach per stack.
- **It gives a stronger kind of proof.** A browser that actually clicks Convert and lands on the next page proves the journey by running it, which beats reading code. It's also slower and flakier: tests that click through a UI break often.
- **Quick visual edits are someone else's market.** Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Cursor's visual editing already compete for "point at the UI and change it", and `HANDOFF.md` notes they own that screen. Codemap's edge is checked wiring, not pixels.

## How I'd test it cheaply
1. **Static journey map first:** pages, actions, navigation and the requests they send, all checkable from the code. It's the same machinery with new kinds of boxes and arrows, which means a deliberate change to the map format.
2. **Show it to Pat and Jay before building more.** A mock journey map of one of their own flows would show whether it helps them steer, or whether what they really want is UX judgement, which is a different product (Jay's note).
3. **Screenshots next:** one image per page, attached to each screen's area. Most of the "see it" value, without live editing.
4. **Pointing at the live UI last,** and only if 1–3 pull hard.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-04 07:03:24Z)**_

Yes. Going by what the interviews point at, I think three ideas beat user journeys. Each builds on what codemap already does well (checking claims against code) instead of adding a new kind of map.

## 1. Plan vs. built: steer the agent while it works (the biggest bet)
Pat lets an agent run for an hour and gets the wrong thing. Patrick finds staying in the loop tiring. Jay worries whether V1 holds up for V2. All three are the same gap: nothing shows whether what got built matches what was intended.

- **Before the build:** turn the plan into a map. Its boxes and arrows are claims with no code behind them yet, so they all show as unconfirmed.
- **During the build:** the checker re-runs as files change, and claims turn green as the code appears. Without reading any code, you see "8 of 12 built, and the arrow from checkout to payments is still missing."
- **When it drifts:** a planned arrow that never appears, or a connection nobody planned, stands out straight away. That's the moment to step in, not an hour later.

It reuses the checker unchanged. The map format needs one deliberate addition: claims that are planned and have no evidence yet. For Jay, a planned V2 map over today's code shows exactly what V2 would have to change.

## 2. Re-check saved maps after every agent run (the cheapest)
`codemap check` already exists and makes no model calls, so it's fast and free. Running it automatically when a coding agent finishes would say "this change broke 2 claims on the signup map" or "the welcome email gap is now closed". That's observability for the people who won't read the code, and it starts the "this step was patched 5 times this week" counter from `HANDOFF.md`. In Claude Code it would be a hook, which I'd check the docs for rather than guess. Probably days of work, not weeks.

## 3. Beat "Claude + Mermaid" on its own ground

- **An MCP server:** gives your coding agent codemap tools: "show the map for this flow", "here's what I just built, add it to the map".

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-04 18:01:23Z)**_

I'd keep editing out of codemap's core, but not because edits don't matter. You're right that the friction is in moving back and forth. Codemap writing the code isn't what removes it, though; a one-click handoff to the agent you already use is.

**Why codemap shouldn't be the one editing:**
- **Two editors in one repo collide.** In the workspace, your coding agent is already changing files. If codemap edits too, you get conflicting changes. `CLAUDE.md` already says only one agent edits at a time.
- **Your coding agent does it better.** It can run the tests and the app, follows the repo's conventions, and remembers the whole session. Codemap's fixes are small exact-text replacements from an explainer that can only read.
- **It's a big surface to keep up.** Approve, undo, file-change checks, uncommitted changes, all in competition with tools that do it full time.
- **Your artifact comparison fits.** The value is seeing and steering; the steering just has to reach whoever writes the code, quickly.

**What I'd keep from the current fix feature:** the proposal drawn on the map. Codemap shows the missing connection, Claude proposes the change, and the map draws it as a green dashed arrow beside the exact change. That's the moment that sells it, and no coding agent does that. Only the last step changes:

| Today | In the workspace |
|---|---|
| **Approve** → codemap writes the change | **Send to my agent** → the change, with the boxes, files and gap it's about, goes to your coding agent |
| Codemap re-checks | The repo watcher sees the files change and re-checks; the dashed arrow turns solid when the code really connects |

How "send" works depends on the agent:
- **Claude Code:** pushed into your running session through channels.
- **Others:** "Copy as prompt", pasted into your agent. The MCP tool could also let the agent pick up waiting requests.

**Approve** stays as a fallback when no agent is connected, like the standalone `codemap "question"` use. It's already built, it's safe (refuses if the files changed, offers Undo), and it keeps the demo working. I just wouldn't extend it further: no bigger fixes, no multi-file refactors.

The other friction you mentioned, spinning codemap up and querying it, is separate, and the workspace pieces cover it:
- **Spinning up:** the skill launches codemap.
- **The right map:** the repo watcher brings it up by itself.
- **Seeing your agent's work:** the MCP tool lets your agent put what it built on the map.

The only time you'd go back to your agent's window is to say "do it", and "Send to my agent" removes even that for Claude Code.
